newsitem.title: UK: Heseltine exits race to lead UK Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Heseltine exits race to lead UK Conservatives.

text.p: Former British deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine on Saturday pulled out of the race to replace John Major as leader of the vanquished Conservative Party after being taken to hospital with heart pains.

The 64-year-old Heseltine, one of the most powerful figures in the party and the man who helped topple former prime minister Margaret Thatcher, had long harboured ambitions to lead the Conservatives and was regarded as a front-runner in the leadership contest after Major decided to stand down.
His decision not to stand leaves wide open the battle to take charge of the party and lead it out of the ruins of its worst electoral defeat for more than 150 years.

"Michael Heseltine suffered mild angina pains early this morning and is now in hospital having tests," the Conservative Central office said in a statement. "He has not had a heart attack and hopes to be home in a few days."
Horton General Hospital in Banbury, central England, said he was comfortable but would remain under observation over the weekend.
Heseltine, whose dashing style and mane of blond hair earned him the nickname "Tarzan", suffered a mild heart attack in 1993.

Hong Kong governor Chris Patten also ruled himself out of the race to replace Major. He said he was "flattered" by suggestions that he could take the job but would take time off after his term as governor ends on June 30.

The scale of the Conservatives' defeat in the May 1 election wiped out many potential leadership candidates. Leading right-winger Michael Portillo, who had been widely touted as a future party leader, unexpectedly lost his seat.
Former foreign secretary Malcom Rifkind, another politician with leadership ambitions, was also unseated as Tony Blair's Labour Party triumphed after 18 years in opposition.

The battle to replace Major is expected to be a bloody one -- the Conservative Party remains deeply divided over Europe and the Eurosceptic right and pro-integration left will both be determined to take control of the party's destiny.

Only former chancellor (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke has so far announced plans to contest the leadership race, but he is deeply disliked by many Eurosceptic Conservatives for his sympathetic stance towards Brussels.

Other likely contenders include right-winger John Redwood, who unsuccessfully tried to unseat Major in 1995, as well as former home secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard and the centrist former health secretary Stephen Dorrell.
William Hague, the 36-year-old former Welsh secretary, is seen as a rising star in the party and may also stand.

Heseltine's decision not to stand probably spells the end of his career at the top of politics, political analysts said. He was tipped for years as a likely Conservative leader but despite wielding significant power as deputy prime minister in Major's government, he never won the top job.
He challenged Thatcher for the party leadership in 1990, but although he succeeded in toppling the "Iron Lady" he lost to Major in the leadership race after Thatcher withdrew.
